solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Initially runs off with politician for sexual high jinks

indicators.note: 'initially' means at the start, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

parts.note: the first letters of these two words
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician runs off in a hurry after a tabloid sex scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs off' reads as fleeing, but it only supplies two first letters. A romp is the tabloid word for a sexual escapade.
explanation.definitionFit: Tabloid newspapers call a frivolous sexual encounter a romp, the noun for playful boisterous fun.

clue.text: Some jobshare politicians turned up for work

indicators.note: in a down answer, turning something up makes it read from bottom to top
'some' takes only part of what follows, so the letters sit inside a longer run of text

parts.note: the letters spanning the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Politicians sharing a job have turned up for work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned up for work' reads as arriving at the office; 'work' is the definition, and the hidden letters run backwards. Latin opus means work, plural opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Opera comes from the Latin plural of opus, and it is also a musical composition, a work in the artistic sense.

clue.text: Carefully select spinach cooked in stew

indicators.note: to be in a stew is to be in a state of confusion, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fussy cook chooses spinach carefully to put in a stew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooked' looks like part of the recipe, and like an anagram signal, but it is fodder: SPINACH plus COOKED makes all thirteen letters, and 'in stew' does the mixing.
explanation.definitionFit: To pick and choose is the idiom for selecting fastidiously, taking only the items one likes best.

clue.text: Teacher with good ability to listen produces mortarboard?

parts.note: the head teacher runs a school
G is the abbreviation for good
an ear for music is an ability to listen well

explanation.surface: A headmaster who listens well earns an academic cap.
explanation.walkthrough: A mortarboard is the square flat academic cap; the question mark flags it as one example of a wider category.
explanation.definitionFit: A mortarboard is one kind of hat, and headgear is the general word for anything worn on the head.

clue.text: Exciting expression of joy spread by promotional item

indicators.note: something spread apart by an insert has that insert sitting in its middle

parts.note: an exclamation of delight
an ad is an advertisement

explanation.surface: Delight spreads thanks to a clever marketing gimmick.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation splits after its second letter to let the advert in.
explanation.definitionFit: Heady describes something intoxicating or thrilling, giving a rush of strong feeling like excitement.

clue.text: Craftsperson taking sides, ousting leader

indicators.note: to oust the leader is to throw out whoever is at the front, so the first letter goes

parts.note: a partisan is committed to one side

explanation.surface: A skilled worker joins a faction that is overthrowing its chief.
explanation.walkthrough: PARTISAN loses its P to leave the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An artisan is a skilled manual worker who makes things by hand, a direct synonym for a crafts worker.

clue.text: Flowery garden on quilt redesigned

indicators.note: something redesigned has its parts rearranged into a new pattern

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A quilt has been redesigned with a floral garden pattern on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flowery' suits a garden quilt, but here it means ornate language.
explanation.definitionFit: Flowery prose is elaborate and pompous in style, which is what grandiloquent speech or writing is.

clue.text: A keen follower receiving rice mostly from Nigeria, say

indicators.note: 'mostly' means most but not all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to receive something is to take it in, so one part goes inside another

parts.note: a fan is an enthusiastic follower
rice without its last letter

explanation.surface: An enthusiast takes delivery of most of a rice shipment from Nigeria.
explanation.walkthrough: The supporter takes the shortened grain inside after its first letter. 'Say' marks Nigeria as just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Nigeria is one country on the continent, so someone or something from there is an example of the adjective.

clue.text: Inclination to write slogan for supporters?

parts.note: to pen is to write
football supporters sing chants from the terraces

explanation.surface: A fan feels the urge to compose a new terrace slogan.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers the slightly loose definition of a chant as a supporters' slogan.
explanation.definitionFit: A penchant is a fondness or liking for something, which is a habitual leaning or tendency.

clue.text: Distinctive character not entirely perceived by the ears

indicators.note: something not entirely there is missing a part, here its final letter

parts.note: aural means relating to hearing

explanation.surface: A personality that cannot quite be sensed by listening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perceived by the ears' sounds like a homophone signal, but it is a plain definition of a word that is then cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: An aura is the distinctive atmosphere or quality that seems to surround a person or place.

clue.text: Happy to host loose group of stars

indicators.note: a host takes guests in, so one part is held inside another

parts.note: gay in its older sense of cheerful
lax means slack or loose

explanation.surface: Someone is pleased to welcome a scattered bunch of celebrities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stars' suggests celebrities at a party, but they are the astronomical kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A galaxy is a huge system of millions of stars bound by gravity, such as the Milky Way.

clue.text: Male supporting generally empty exercise venue

indicators.note: in a down answer, a support sits underneath, so this part goes last
an empty word has had its insides removed, leaving only the outside letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
M is the abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: A man backs a plan for a fitness centre that is usually deserted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Generally empty' reads as 'usually deserted', but 'generally' is the source word and 'empty' strips it.
explanation.definitionFit: A gym, short for gymnasium, is a hall or club equipped for physical training and workouts.

clue.text: Corrupt French nobleman interrupting witness

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into the middle of something, so one part sits inside another

parts.note: to witness is to see
duc is French for duke

explanation.surface: A crooked French aristocrat keeps interrupting a court witness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corrupt' looks like an adjective for the nobleman, but it is the verb definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To seduce someone is to lead them astray, tempting them into wrongdoing, which is to corrupt them.

clue.text: Daughter in Mile End disrupted grand district for conservative constituency?

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it
something disrupted is thrown into disorder, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written; Mile End is a district of east London
G is short for grand, slang for a thousand pounds
D is the abbreviation for daughter
a land is a region or territory

explanation.surface: A daughter living in a run-down part of east London moves to a posh conservative area.
explanation.walkthrough: The daughter goes into the place name before the letters are mixed. 'Constituency' is meant loosely: a body of supporters, not an electoral seat, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Middle England is the label for the conservative-leaning middle-class population outside big cities, a political bloc rather than a place.

clue.text: Ape? One friend cages it

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: a cage encloses whatever is put in it, so one part surrounds another

parts.note: a mate is a friend
taken as written

explanation.surface: A monkey is locked up by a pal who keeps it caged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ape' looks like the animal kept in the cage, but it is the verb meaning to copy.
explanation.definitionFit: To ape someone is to copy their manner or behaviour, often mockingly, a verb sense of the animal.

clue.text: Times journalists backing English state

indicators.note: in a down answer, what backs something sits beneath it, so these parts come after

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
x is the multiplication sign
the press is journalists collectively

explanation.surface: Reporters on the Times newspaper support the English nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the newspaper, which suits 'journalists', but it is the multiplication sign. 'State' is a verb, not a nation.
explanation.definitionFit: To express a view is to put it into words, to declare or say it plainly.

clue.text: Dorothy cuddled Toto right at the end

indicators.note: 'at the end' points to the last position, so only each word's final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letters of these three words

explanation.surface: In The Wizard of Oz, Dorothy hugs her dog Toto at the end of the film.
explanation.walkthrough: The scene is from The Wizard of Oz, where Toto is the heroine's dog; 'right' looks like 'correctly' but just gives its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Dot is a common pet form or short nickname for the given name Dorothy.

clue.text: Religious leader is hot in dance

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: a bop is an informal dance
taken as written
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A churchman gets heated at the disco.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' looks like the link, but it joins H as the filling of the dance.
explanation.definitionFit: A bishop is a senior member of the clergy in charge of a diocese, a leader within a church.

clue.text: Perform joke, mostly in stage turn

indicators.note: 'mostly' means most but not all, so the final letter is dropped
one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: an act is a turn performed on stage
a quip is a joke, here cut short

explanation.surface: A comedian tells a gag during a variety slot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perform' looks like it belongs to the comic act, but it is the definition, in the sense of 'acquit yourself well'.
explanation.definitionFit: To acquit oneself is to behave or do a task in a particular way, so it means to conduct oneself or carry out.

clue.text: Secretary upset friend in shock

indicators.note: to upset something is to tip it over, so in a down answer it reads upwards

parts.note: a PA is a personal assistant
a pal is a friend

explanation.surface: An office secretary is distressed at a shocking event involving a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' reads as distressed, but it turns the assistant over.
explanation.definitionFit: To appal is to horrify or dismay someone, a verb synonym for giving people a nasty jolt.

clue.text: End of report missing from paper edition

indicators.note: something missing from a whole has been taken out of it

parts.note: tissue is thin soft paper

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A newspaper edition goes out without the final part of a report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paper' suggests a newspaper, which suits 'edition', but it is tissue paper.
explanation.definitionFit: An issue is one number of a periodical published at a particular time, the same as an edition.

clue.text: Golden circle not quite 50% round

indicators.note: 'not quite' falls just short, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: fifty per cent is half, cut short
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A gold ring that is not quite half round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like part of the geometry of the circle, but it is just the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: A halo is the ring of light painted around the head of a saint, traditionally shown in gold.

clue.text: Coffee: French are to urge termination of Americano

parts.note: es is French for 'are', as in tu es
to press someone is to urge them

indicators.note: a termination is an ending, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: French café owners are pushing to scrap the Americano from the menu.
explanation.walkthrough: An Americano is itself a coffee, which makes 'termination of Americano' read as ending its sale.
explanation.definitionFit: Espresso is strong black coffee made by forcing steam through ground beans, one kind of the drink.

clue.text: Disclosure about Royal Society is a setback

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so one part surrounds another

parts.note: a reveal is a disclosure
RS is the abbreviation for the Royal Society

explanation.surface: A revelation about Britain's scientific academy proves a blow to it.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Society is Britain's national academy of sciences. 'Disclosure' is used as a noun, matching the modern noun reveal.
explanation.definitionFit: A reversal is a change of fortune for the worse, a defeat or blow just like a setback.

clue.text: Fix right level

parts.note: to tie is to fasten or fix
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fix right' reads as 'correct properly', but it splits into a verb and an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A tier is one of a series of rows or layers placed one above another, such as a rank.
